bodyContrast.why: WCAG 1.4.3 for text under 18px. Both systems set body at 15px, so the body floor is the one that binds.

graphicalContrast.why: WCAG 1.4.11 for non-text objects. An axis or a connector has to be findable against its ground without being as loud as type.

recessiveDeltaEOK.why: Perceptual distance from its own ground for a mark that is meant to recede. A baseline rule under a bar chart is not an axis you hunt for; the mark carries the data and the rule only says where zero is. Holding it to the 3:1 graphical floor would forbid a legitimate and common treatment, and exempting it entirely would let a rule vanish into the page. On a white ground it rejects a rule measured at 0.0152 dE while admitting one measured at 0.0332 dE. The number 0.03 is the same figure the ramp-step floor uses, but not the same measure: scaleStepDeltaL is OKLab lightness alone, while this one is full OKLab distance.

seriesDeltaEOK.why: Perceptual distance in OKLab between any two categorical series. Luminance contrast is the wrong measure: one system separates series by hue and the other by value, and a luminance test would reject the chromatic pair while passing an illegible neutral one.

markDeltaEOK.why: The mark says this value differs from its neighbours. Same measure as series and the same reason: the contract expresses the emphasis job, not the emphasis mechanism.

ruleWeightFloor.why: The lightest a division may be drawn, in px. A deck is a fixed 1280 canvas that gets exported and projected, and a rule under half a pixel disappears in both. This is the floor on the brand's freedom, not on the kit's: the kit only ever says which step a division takes.

ruleWeightCeiling.why: The heaviest a division may be drawn, in px. Past roughly six the line stops dividing two things and becomes a third thing between them, which changes what the page argues rather than how it looks. A brand that wants a heavy rule gets six; a brand that wants a block wants a panel, and panels are a different token.

panelRadiusCeiling.why: The largest corner radius a tinted panel may take, in px. A commentary rail is a zone of the page, and past roughly 24 on a 1280 canvas it detaches into a card floating above the page instead. The cap exists so a brand can be as soft as it likes without the layout's zoning turning into a set of widgets.

scaleStepDeltaL.why: Adjacent steps of an ordinal or sequential scale must be separable, but a scale is read as a ramp against its own neighbours rather than as independent categories, so the bar sits below the series bar. Measured in OKLab lightness alone, not full OKLab distance: a sequential ramp encodes magnitude, magnitude is read as lightness, and letting chroma pay for lightness would hold a chromatic system to a weaker bar than a neutral one, where chroma cannot substitute.

surface.description: The grounds a page and its panels sit on, and the rules that divide them. Ground is the page, surface is a panel raised off it, well is a recessed field. Rule-firm is the divider held to a contrast floor; rule is a quieter division that is not. Rule-strong is the heaviest division a page draws, above rule-firm: a booktabs boundary or a threshold that has to read as a statement rather than as scaffolding. Held to the same non-text floor as rule-firm, and expected to sit well above it.

text.description: Type colour by job, not by size. Muted is secondary and label type, strong is the emphatic end, on-field is type over a full-bleed divider.

exhibit.description: Exhibit primitives. Axis is structure you must be able to find and is held to the non-text contrast floor; axis-quiet is a rule that recedes, held only to being perceptible against its ground. Connector is structure, held to the same non-text contrast floor as axis. Fill is the default mark body, fill-quiet is a recessive tint used behind or beside a mark rather than as a mark body carrying data on its own. Label-muted is tick and axis type. A connector also covers structure drawn at a mark to separate it from the field behind it, which is the same thin-structure job at the same floor.

scales.description: Three scales with three different jobs. Ordinal encodes rank across four levels. Sequential encodes magnitude across five steps and must ramp monotonically. Series encodes category across three lines and must be mutually separable rather than ordered.

mark.description: The single marked value on an exhibit. Mark is the body, mark-soft is the field a mark sits on so the mark still reads against it, mark-text is type carried on the mark. A mark must also stand apart from every categorical series, because a chart carrying both devices puts them side by side and a marked value that is the colour of a category is not marked. It must also stand apart from every step of every scale. A mark says this value differs from its neighbours; a scale says this value is larger than its neighbours. A mark that is the colour of a magnitude is making the second claim while meaning the first.

field.description: The full-bleed colour field of a divider or statement page, and the type carried on it. Field-text-muted is secondary type on a full-bleed field, where field-text is the primary. A cover carries a title and a kicker and the kicker has to recede without falling below the body floor.

separation.description: How a panel separates from its ground. Components set both, always. One system supplies a real border and no shadow, the other the reverse, and no component ever branches.

type.description: Three families, ten sizes, five weights, four tracking values bound to size band, and leading on a four-pixel baseline. A system with one family aliases all three family names to it.

line.description: How heavily a division is drawn, as three steps. The kit chooses which step each division takes, because the hierarchy between divisions is structure: a booktabs boundary has to read heavier than a row divider or the table stops being a table. The brand chooses what each step measures, because absolute weight is identity, and a house that rules at a hairline and a house that rules at three pixels are drawing the same structure in their own hand. Held to hair <= bold <= heavy so a brand cannot invert the hierarchy, and to a floor and ceiling so a division cannot vanish or become a block.

shape.description: Corner treatment, named by what the corner belongs to rather than by a size. Panel is a tinted field carrying reading: a commentary rail, a KPI band, an annotation strip, the ink finding. Hard corners and soft corners are one of the loudest signals of whose deck this is, and until 2026-08-31 the kit drew no radius anywhere and a rounded house could not be expressed at all. Capped, because past a point a tinted zone stops reading as a zone and starts reading as a card. Data marks are deliberately NOT offered a radius yet: a rounded bar end shortens the bar a reader measures, so that one needs its own decision rather than a token.

space.description: Ten steps on a four-pixel base. No value exists between them.

geometry.description: The slide profile. Declared per system rather than defaulted, because one system is a document that also renders slides and the other is being changed to slide-first.

art.description: A string prepended to every image prompt, so the two brands do not produce imagery that reads as the same model.

identity.description: The firm's name, drawn once per working slide in the padding band. A string token on the precedent art sets: a value the kit must print and must not know. Slide.astro carried one firm's name as a literal until 2026-08-28, which made it the last brand value inside the kit and would have printed that firm on the other one's piece.

ordered.why: The kit draws a row divider at hair, an emphatic division at bold and the loudest division a page carries at heavy, and it reads the hierarchy back out of that ordering. A brand that sets bold lighter than hair has not restyled the deck, it has inverted what the deck says about which division matters.
